newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Philippine borrowers shine in debt markets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Philippine borrowers shine in debt markets.

text.p: Philippine corporate borrowers are riding high on the crest of a resurgent economy, as international creditors favour them with longer repayment periods and lower interest charges.

Since their return to the international bond market in early 1993, Filipino companies have issued more than $4.0 billion worth of Eurobonds, Euro certificates of deposits (CDs), global bonds, floating rate notes, Euro convertible bonds and Yankee bonds.

"The Philippines' access to the international capital market has really been exemplary," Simon Paterno, vice president and representative of the Manila office of JP Morgan Securities Asia, told Reuters.

Philippine names were shunned by the capital market for 10 years from 1983 when the Philippine government declared a debt payment moratorium following a vast capital flight as the rule of president Ferdinand Marcos withered. By then, the country's net international reserves had declined to a negative $1.82 billion.
After Marcos was forced out of power in 1986 through a people's revolution, debt markets slowly began regaining confidence in the economy.

The reform of the Philippine economy through liberalisation and deregulation of vital industries was capped by the successful restructuring of the country's foreign commercial loans through a Brady deal in December 1992.
A three-year, $150 million Eurobond was launched within two months, marking the return of the country to the international capital market.

The JP Morgan-led bond carried a stiff interest rate of 250 basis points above that of the U.S. Treasury but immediately after listing, the Eurobonds were actively bought in the secondary market at a premium.
BLUE CHIP COMPANIES JOIN THE FRAY

In the span of the last four years, Philippine blue-chip companies have joined in the fray, led by the giant Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co (PLDT) and the state-owned National Power Corp (Napocor), both of which needed long-term financing to bankroll their expansion programmes.
PLDT issued seven-year and 10-year Yankee bonds in June 1996 while Napocor issued 10-year and 20-year Yankee bonds in December 1996.

"There's a pent-up demand for capital from companies and banks in the Philippines. From October 1983, when the country went into the debt rescheduling phase, until it got out of it in late 1992, the country basically lost all access to the private capital market," Paterno said.

In the Euro-CD market, the Philippine Commercial International Bank (PCIBank) made the initial entry with $30-million, three-month Euro-CDs collateralised with Brady bonds months after the country's first Eurobond. The CDs were offered at the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) plus 150 basis points.
Last September, the same bank issued five-year, $100-million fixed-rate CDs only 120 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
PCIBank executive vice president Esperanza Osmena said the Philippine banks' CDs were well-received, especially among other financial institutions and institutional investors based in Asia.
She pointed out that even middle-sized banks were venturing into Euro-CDs with tight spreads to fund their foreign exchange requirements.
"Even unrated companies are able to tap the Eurobond market," added Johnny Noe Ravalo, chief economist at the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP).
RATING UPGRADE EXPECTED

"Despite the higher level of debt issuance...the Philippines has been able to borrow at levels well below the average spread for emerging markets debt of 284 basis points. The average spread for Philipine debt has narrowed significantly to a range of 150 to 250 basis points compared to a range of 250 to 375 basis points during the 1993-1995 period," Joyce Chang of Merrill Lynch said in a recent report.
The country's external debt stood at 51 percent of gross national product (GNP) last year, down from 120 percent of GNP at the height of the external debt crisis in 1985.

Debt service has likewise declined relative to the country's capacity to pay. From a high of 30 to 40 percent of exports of goods and services in the mid-1980s, debt service declined in proportion to 11.6 percent of exports of goods and services in 1995. It is expected to dip to 10.6 percent this year.
Debt-service ratios and debt-to-GNP ratios are two of the critical measures which have been mentioned frequently as benchmarks being tracked by international creditors.
The market consensus is that the Philippines will receive a credit upgrade within the year, or in 1998 at the latest. The country is currently rated as Ba2 by Moody's and BB by Standard & Poor's.

A recent Bankers Trust report said the pending upgrade had several U.S. pension funds and insurance companies taking a closer look at Philippine paper, since they are now allowed to take positions in "cross over" situations where the securities rated just below investment grade have generally a positive outlook.
30-YEAR YANKEE BOND AND EUROPESO MULLED
At present, investment banks are scrambling to lead manage a 30-year Yankee bond planned by the government.

Among those which have expressed interest are JP Morgan, Citicorp, Morgan Stanley, ING Baring, CS First Boston, Goldman Sachs Global Income Fund, Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc, Salomon Bros Fund Inc, Salomon Brothers Investment Fund Inc, Banker's Trust and Merrill Lynch.
"Unlike in the past, it's the investment banks which are aggressively pursuing the national government to tap the Yankee market," said Rosalia de Leon, director of the Department of Finance.
Foreign investment banks were also actively courting oil refiner Petron Corp and the utility firm Manila Electric Co to underwrite their debut debt papers.
Aside from Yankee bonds, investment banks were also looking at issuing Euro-peso bonds for foreign investors, dealers said.
